mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Supay ‌place ​underworld, death ​at ​the ​center of ​a ‌living ​mythological world.

### ​Origins ‌(Myth)

​Supay appears ‌in ​incan ‌tradition as ​underworld, ​death. ​The name's ​meaning, ​"The ‌spirit", shapes ​the ‌narratives ​told about ‌this ​figure.

### ‌Worship and ​Memory ‌(Cult)

​Devotees and ​later ‌tradition-keepers ‌preserved Supay ‌in ​ritual, ​text, and ‌iconography, ​ensuring ​the name ‌survived ​into ​the modern ‌scholarly ​record.

The ‌myths ​of ​Supay survive ​in ​fragments, ‌summaries, and ‌later ​retellings. ‌Each version ​reflects ​the ‌interests of ‌its ‌tellers ‌— poets, ​priests, ‌philosophers, ​and scholars. ​The ​PuniCodex ‌entry does ​not ​privilege ​a single ‌version; ​it ​gathers the ​attestations ‌so ​that readers ‌can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Supay ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

archaeology.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Supay ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Incan ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Supay, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​underworld ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Supay** ​(*supay*) — ‌Underworld, Death ‌· ​The spirit ​— belongs ​to the ​Incan ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Underworld, ​Death". The ‌name ​means "The ‌spirit"[^1].

**Supay** ​is ​the lord ​of *uku ​pacha*, ​the inner ‌world beneath ​the Andes ‌— ​the domain ‌of the ​dead, ‌of cave-dwelling ​spirits, and ‌of ​the mineral ​wealth the ‌earth conceals. ‌No ‌temple bore ​his name; ​he ‌was propitiated, ​not praised. ​Under Spanish ‌rule ​the name ​was reforged: ‌*supay* ​became the ‌Quechua word ​for ​'devil', and ​the lord ​of the ‌inner ‌world survives ​today as ‌the ​miners' *Tío*.[^2]

​PuniCodex records ‌the canonical ‌scholarly ‌spelling **Supay** ‌and serves ​its ‌temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/supay/). ​The ​displayed form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description ​computed from ‌the displayed ​form ​itself. The ​plain ASCII ‌form ​*supay* contains ‌the same ​letters: no ‌recovered ​diacritics or ‌special encoding ‌is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
No ​indigenous ‌written attestation ‌survives ​for ​this name; ​**Supay** ​is ​a scholarly ‌transliteration ​of ​the ‌reconstructed spoken ​form. ‌Etymologically ​the name ‌means ​"The ​spirit"[^1].

​The canonical ​spelling ​**Supay** ‌matches the ​conventional ‌scholarly ​romanization. The ‌plain ​ASCII ‌form ​*supay* contains ‌the ​same ​letters, so ‌no ‌lost ‌diacritics ​or encoding ​transition ‌is ​claimed. The ​editorial ‌work ​is to ​fix ‌one ​reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ​capitalization ​and provenance, ​and ‌keep ‌the original ​evidence ‌visible. ​The ​displayed form ‌is ‌ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ‌description ​computed ‌from ​the displayed ​form ​itself.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ​**s** → ‌**S** ​— ​Same, ​capitalized
- **u** ‌→ ​**u** ‌— Same
- ​**p** ‌→ ​**p** ‌— Same
- ‌**a** ​→ ​**a** — ​Same
- ​**y** ‌→ **y** ‌— ​Same

meditation.body:
Supay ​is the ‌lord of ‌the underground ​who ​was renamed ​but never ​dethroned. ​Colonial priests ‌thought that ​calling him ​'devil' ‌would finish ​him; instead ‌the ​name became ‌a mask, ​and behind ​the ​mask the ​old contract ​continued ‌in the ​dark of ‌the mines. ​There ‌is a ​lesson in ‌the ​economics of ‌belief here: ​a power ​that ‌controls what ‌you need ‌— ​passage for ​your dead, ‌safety for ​your ​labor, metal ‌for your ​markets ​— cannot ‌be argued ​away. It ‌can ​only be ​paid.

The ​restoration ​of *Supay* ‌is therefore ‌more than ​philological ‌courtesy. It ​returns to ​the ‌figure his ‌own name, ‌before the ‌extirpators ​rewrote it, ‌and it ​asks ​the reader ​to hold ‌both histories ​at ​once: the ​lord of ‌uku ​pacha and ​the colonial ​devil, the ‌cave ​offerings and ‌the Tuesday ​cigarettes ‌at Cerro ​Rico. The ‌earth, this ‌name ​insists, keeps ​its own ​accounts, ​and its ‌oldest creditor ‌is still ​collecting.[^1]
